timing: Editorial cue timings retained from the original animation; English narration is a translation and is not aligned to a recorded voice.

cues.narration: The concept behind the project dates back to before the 1990s.
cues.visual: 1987: a detector sketch in the ice and an idea symbol appear.

cues.narration: Early tests were carried out in Greenland.
cues.visual: 1990: a schematic Greenland map, test borehole, and optical sensors appear.

cues.narration: In 1999, IceCube was formally proposed to the United States National Science Foundation, or NSF.
cues.visual: 1999: a detector drawing becomes a proposal document and moves toward the NSF symbol.
2004: hot-water drilling advances through an ice cross-section.

cues.narration: and the first detector string was installed in 2005.
cues.visual: 2005: the first sensor string is lowered into a borehole.

cues.narration: Two neutrino events were detected with that first string.
cues.visual: Two separate upward-going muon tracks are recorded beside the first string.
The camera expands from one string to the full array as the final strings are added.

cues.narration: Evidence for astrophysical neutrinos was announced in 2013.
cues.visual: The array becomes a publication page with dots representing the 28-event sample.

cues.narration: Two exceptionally energetic neutrinos had already been detected in 2011 and 2012.
cues.visual: The timeline moves backward to two separate cascade events in 2011 and 2012.

cues.narration: They were nicknamed Bert and Ernie.
cues.visual: The two events remain side by side with their internationally used names.

cues.narration: Those two events alone, however, were not enough to establish a distant cosmic origin conclusively.
cues.visual: The records connect to atmospheric and distant-space possibilities, with question marks indicating uncertainty.
